title: AI Solves a Major Unsolved Math Problem. Not Everyone Is Happy
key_facts: IEEE Spectrum (freelance writer Benjamin Skuse, 5 Oct 2026) reports from the Heidelberg Laureate Forum in Germany, which opened on 13 Sep 2026 for a week; talk there was dominated by AI companies' advances in mathematics.

OpenAI claims to have solved the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of seven Millennium Prize Problems set in 2000 by the Clay Mathematics Institute; only the Poincaré conjecture has been solved by humans. The article says the claim, if verified, would be a watershed moment for automated reasoning.

Fields Medalist Jacob Tsimerman (University of Toronto) said AI capabilities have risen faster than many people expected and, while saying he did not know the details, that solving Navier-Stokes feels pretty definitive.

Fields Medalist Peter Scholze (University of Bonn) said the AI companies are solving such problems as benchmarks, as some kind of PR stunt; Geordie Williamson (University of Sydney) said OpenAI behaved extremely poorly; Michael Harris (Columbia) said most reports depict OpenAI as bullying and disrupting norms.

NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, who was working on Navier-Stokes with Anthropic's Levent Alpöge, claimed correspondence with OpenAI that appeared coercive, censorious and even threatening. OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment before publication.
Williamson says understanding and solved problems are becoming uncorrelated, so how people are assessed, who gets jobs and how people are educated must be reevaluated.

Mita Ramabulana (University of Cape Town) said two of the 10 advances OpenAI announced in August overlapped with his own work; Ailsa Robertson (University of Amsterdam) said colleagues use LLMs intensively, some spending thousands of euros on extra tokens, after OpenAI announced in July 100,000 free licences for academic researchers.
Rumours: Anthropic used an unreleased Claude on the Riemann hypothesis in August and made progress on a related problem but not the main goal; OpenAI is reportedly focusing on the Hodge conjecture.
quote_evidence: OpenAI’s claim to have solved a second, the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, if verified, represents a watershed moment for automated reasoning.
“I think that OpenAI behaved extremely poorly, and that we should acknowledge that in the community,” said Williamson.

“They’re really just solving these difficult mathematical problems as benchmarks, as some kind of PR stunt,” opined Fields Medalist Peter Scholze, of the University of Bonn, in Germany, during a panel discussion at the event about AI in mathematical research.
why_it_matters_hint: Mathematicians, especially early-career ones, describe pressure to use costly AI tools, overlap with AI-announced results and a needed rethink of hiring and teaching (Williamson); the Navier-Stokes claim itself is still unverified.
event_date: OpenAI announced its Navier-Stokes claim on 8 Sep 2026 (BBC); the forum began 13 Sep 2026; the article is dated 5 Oct 2026.
notes: Read in full (fulltext file). The article gives no date for OpenAI's claim and no 88 hours; those come from the BBC report of 8 Sep 2026 (read in full): about 10,000 AI agents, 88 hours, not independently verified or accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute; Buckmaster said information on his work was passed to OpenAI, OpenAI said it had not seen their work. The pool linked this item to 5 Oct pool item 'OpenAI says AI agents solved centuries-old mathematical problem in 88 hours' (ANA, 4 Oct 2026), which is the same 8 Sep claim reported late; neither appears in any edition we printed since 23 Sep (archive checked). The article is a feature on the reaction to older news.
